_label: Evidence archive: screenshots of the studio's outreach, 12-13 September 2013

identified_by.content: Evidence archive: screenshots of the studio's outreach, 12-13 September 2013

content: Three screenshots, held by the studio, taken on the studio principal's Mac over two afternoons in September 2013, the same two days as the letter to a university art museum recorded in the 2013 museum-correspondence record. The first shows a discussion he had just started in a private LinkedIn group, 'Arts & Crafts Professional', under the title '"Art Market Reform": Promoting Art Tax on the local, state, national, and international levels to encourage and promote accountability, transparency, and regulation in the Art Market and Art World', posted as Joseph Chirum, Chief Executive Artist at Sun and Rain Works; the group's activity panel dates the post '1 minute ago'. The second shows the same browser open at the Sotheby's website's list of its locations worldwide. The third shows the studio's webmail open at a reply from the Assistant Director of the Oregon Arts Commission, the State of Oregon's arts agency, headed 'RE: Metaconceptual Art project discussion follow up' and dated in the mail client Fri, Sep 13, 2013 at 2:58 PM. The reply thanks him for sharing his work, points him to the Commission's grants for individual artists and nonprofits, and wishes him 'the best on your proposal to the White House'. Together they show the studio carrying the same declaration to a professional network and to a state arts agency in the same days it wrote to the museum. They are the studio's own screenshots of its own outreach, and the one reply they show is a courtesy referral.

referred_to_by.content: Evidence status: held by the studio as screenshots only, with no machine metadata of their own. Each file is a 1,280 by 800 pixel PNG carrying nothing but an embedded colour profile and a pixel-density field: no capture date, no software tag, no XMP, and none of the 'Screenshot' marker a Mac writes into a screenshot it saves. They were therefore re-saved or passed through some other tool before reaching the studio's current archive, and their file dates describe when they were copied, not when they were taken. The embedded profile is the Mac's own display profile, which macOS generated on 2013-01-06 at 15:51:44, and it is identical in all three files; that is a floor under all three, if the profile belongs to the machine that took them, and evidence that one machine took all three. The held originals are f0040080.png (the LinkedIn screenshot), 759,660 bytes, SHA-256 7d2a0d0b61a77b3aea8a77761249fce228d9f0bc9e65a043fc642045a85fd725; f0046672.png (the Sotheby's page), 436,785 bytes, SHA-256 6e63fa6e87745923f07ffd45961609bc93c4d8a7f562254b0f0062959325f991; and f0047824.png (the Arts Commission reply), 436,804 bytes, SHA-256 48e65d283878e9e09ecc7ce40516b76750a93a0d977149b1b01fa66eae5facac.

How the dates are fixed, and how firmly. Only one date in the set is printed in full: the mail client's header on the Arts Commission reply, Fri, Sep 13, 2013, 2:58 PM. The screenshot of it shows the Mac's menu-bar clock at Fri 3:09 PM, eleven minutes later, and the dock's calendar icon at 13. The Sotheby's screenshot shows Fri 2:46 PM with the calendar at 13, the same four other tabs open in the same order, and the webmail tab's unread count one lower, 3,329 against 3,330, so it was taken twenty-three minutes before the reply screenshot on the same afternoon. The LinkedIn screenshot shows Thu 3:49 PM with the calendar at 12, the same browser and menu-bar items, and the LinkedIn post is still open as a tab in both Friday screenshots; it is dated to Thursday 12 September 2013 by that sequence, not by anything printed in it. The browser's appearance is Firefox before its redesign of April 2014, which agrees. On those grounds the set is dated 12-13 September 2013; the Friday dates are read from the screen and the Thursday date is inferred from them. The times are the Mac's local clock, which this record takes to have been on Pacific time; on that assumption the LinkedIn post went up about half an hour before the first message to the museum, whose headers place it at 16:19 Pacific the same day.

The LinkedIn post, in its own words. The post opens: 'My name is Joseph M. Chirum, and i am writing to begin, encourage, and promote an open discussion regarding "Art Market Reform" and "Art Tax".' It then says that in May 2009 he auctioned lot 16 of Sotheby's New York photograph auction, Ansel Adams's 'San Francisco from Twin Peaks', 'as a performance act of Metaconceptual Art'; that Metaconceptual Art has eight defining characteristics findable on Google or YouTube; that he had submitted a proposal for 'Art Market Reform' and 'Art Tax' to the White House two days earlier and was awaiting feedback; and that when they spoke on the telephone he was asked to find local parties and support for the proposal, which is the purpose of the discussion. The wording follows the museum letter of the same afternoon closely, including the May dating of the sale, which is wrong: Sotheby's sale N08533 took place on 30 March 2009. The error is left as written here, as it is in the museum record. The telephone call and the White House submission are the studio's statements; this collection has not verified either and does not assert them. The studio's LinkedIn profile has no archived copy and can no longer be reached, so this screenshot is the only copy of the post the studio holds.

The Arts Commission reply. The reply is from the Oregon Arts Commission's Assistant Director, with one colleague copied, and answers a message from the studio headed 'Metaconceptual Art project discussion follow up'; a second tab in the same screenshot shows an automatic reply to a message whose subject also begins 'Met'. The studio's own message is not shown. What the reply establishes is narrow: that on 13 September 2013 a state arts agency received the studio's approach about the Metaconceptual Art project, that the studio had told it of a proposal to the White House, and that the agency answered with a referral to its grants programme. It records no endorsement, partnership, funding, or assessment of the work, and none should be inferred. The agency is named because the identity of the recipient is what gives the exchange its weight; the individuals are identified by role only, following this collection's convention.

The Sotheby's page. The second screenshot shows only that the studio had the Sotheby's locations page open on the afternoon of 13 September 2013, beside the LinkedIn post and a Wikipedia list of contemporary art museums. It is not evidence of any contact with Sotheby's in 2013, and none is claimed.

Publication and redaction. The three screenshots are published here as redacted copies: /images/linkedin-art-market-reform-2013.png, /images/sothebys-locations-2013.png and /images/arts-commission-reply-2013.png. The redactions cover the studio's own mailbox names and addresses in the browser's tab and title bars; in the LinkedIn screenshot, the names and photographs of other group members in the 'Top Influencers' and 'Latest Activity' panels; and in the reply, the staff member's name, both staff mailbox addresses, and the direct office telephone number. Nothing else was altered. The published files are re-encoded copies, so their checksums differ from those of the originals given above. The unredacted originals are held by the studio on separate media.

What these screenshots do not show. They are not the messages themselves: no message file with headers is held for the Arts Commission exchange, the sending mailbox is no longer available to the studio, and no copy has been requested from the Commission. They date nothing before September 2013 and are not evidence of the 2007 origin, of the 2009 sale as an artwork, or of any White House submission. The LinkedIn post and the message to the Commission are the artist's own declarations, of the same kind as the museum letter; the one outside voice in the set is a courteous reply that takes no position on the work.
